papers.title: Cellular Mechanisms Enabling Mitochondria Transfer and Transplantation
papers.summary: This paper reviews the cellular mechanisms that allow mitochondria to move between cells, including tunneling nanotubes, extracellular vesicles, and direct transplantation techniques. It covers how donor mitochondria are internalized by recipient cells and integrated into their existing mitochondrial network. The review also discusses therapeutic applications where transferred or transplanted mitochondria rescue cells with mitochondrial dysfunction.
papers.why: Understanding how mitochondria are transferred and internalized provides mechanistic context for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control pathways relevant to interneuron health and resilience in the brain.
papers.figure: A schematic diagram illustrating the different mechanisms of mitochondrial transfer (tunneling nanotubes, vesicle-mediated transfer, and direct transplantation) and their cellular uptake routes.

papers.title: Lysosomes as chemical and metabolic organizers of central nervous system injury and repair
papers.summary: This paper discusses lysosomes as central hubs that coordinate chemical and metabolic processes during central nervous system injury and repair. It likely explores how lysosomal function influences the clearance of damaged cellular components and the regulation of metabolic signaling after neural injury. The work probably ties lysosomal activity to broader recovery mechanisms, including waste degradation pathways relevant to neuronal health.
papers.why: Since lysosomes are essential to autophagy and mitophagy, this paper could provide mechanistic insight into lysosomal regulation of neuronal waste clearance after injury, directly relevant to studying mitophagy in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: Protocol for analyzing autophagy-related cellular phenotypes in autophagy-deficient human embryonic stem cell-derived lacrimal gland-like organoids.
papers.summary: This paper presents a protocol for studying autophagy-related cellular phenotypes using human embryonic stem cell-derived lacrimal gland-like organoids that are deficient in autophagy genes. The method likely details how to generate these organoids, induce autophagy deficiency, and then analyze resulting cellular changes such as organelle accumulation or structural abnormalities. It serves as a methodological resource for researchers studying autophagy dysfunction in a specific tissue model system.
papers.why: While this protocol focuses on lacrimal gland organoids rather than neurons, it may offer transferable methodological approaches for assessing autophagy-deficient phenotypes that could inform techniques for studying mitophagy and autophagy disruption in neuronal or brain tissue contexts.

papers.title: Multi-target neuroprotective mechanisms of epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) in stroke: from molecular pathways to nanomedicine delivery and clinical translation
papers.summary: This paper reviews how EGCG, a green tea compound, protects brain cells after stroke by acting on multiple molecular pathways at once. It covers mechanisms like reducing oxidative stress, inflammation, and cell death, while also discussing new nanomedicine approaches to deliver EGCG more effectively to the brain. The paper also touches on progress toward testing these strategies in clinical settings.
papers.why: While focused on stroke rather than neuron-intrinsic autophagy/mitophagy, EGCG's neuroprotective pathways and delivery strategies could offer tangential insight into pharmacological modulation of autophagy-related neuroprotection relevant to interneuron vulnerability studies.

papers.title: Molecular mechanism and potential role of mitophagy in breast cancer.
papers.summary: This paper discusses mitophagy, the process by which cells selectively degrade damaged mitochondria, and how it relates to breast cancer development and progression. It likely reviews the molecular pathways involved, such as PINK1/Parkin and receptor-mediated mitophagy, and how these pathways influence tumor cell survival, metabolism, and treatment resistance. The abstract itself provides no further experimental details beyond this general scope.
papers.why: While focused on cancer rather than neurons, this paper could offer mechanistic insights into mitophagy pathway regulation that may be transferable to understanding mitochondrial quality control in neurons.

papers.title: Mitophagy-related gene signatures predict prognosis and therapeutic response in hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.summary: This study develops gene expression signatures based on mitophagy-related genes to predict outcomes in liver cancer patients. The researchers link these signatures to patient survival and response to therapeutic treatments. The work is bioinformatics-focused, using mitophagy as a biomarker category in an oncology context rather than studying the process itself in detail.
papers.why: While this paper centers on hepatocellular carcinoma rather than brain tissue, it may offer mitophagy-related gene sets or computational approaches that could inform marker selection for spatial transcriptomics analyses in neuronal studies.

papers.title: A Bibliometric Review of Research Trends and Therapeutic Potential Reveals Natural Products as Major Regulators of Mitophagy in Kidney Disease.
papers.summary: This paper is a bibliometric analysis mapping research trends on mitophagy (mitochondrial autophagy) in kidney disease, identifying key publications, authors, and research hotspots. It highlights that natural products (plant-derived compounds) are emerging as major therapeutic regulators of mitophagy pathways in kidney pathology. The review synthesizes trends rather than presenting new experimental data, focusing on citation networks and topic clustering over time.
papers.why: While focused on kidney rather than brain tissue, this review's bibliometric mapping of mitophagy regulation by natural products could offer transferable insights into therapeutic strategies and methodological trends applicable to neuronal mitophagy research.
